encounters.name: The Inbox Mimic
encounters.room_intro: Torchlight catches a mail alcove in the campus crypt. A chest with envelope-teeth rattles like a new alert, hugging a glowing scroll stamped URGENT TREASURE.

character.name: The Inbox Mimic
character.portrait_hint: A grinning treasure chest with envelope teeth and a peeling fake Federal Student Aid seal.

encounters.scenario:
URGENT, brave Owl! Your leftover Federal Student Aid grant of $3,450 expires at midnight. Reply with your StudentAid.gov password and tap this portal to claim your treasure now!

- Office of Student Treasure
aid-office@ksu-grants-secure.net

choices.label: Inspect sender
choices.fallback_reaction: Hey, quit squinting at my return address! My shiny seal was supposed to dazzle you, not get inspected. Ugh, back in the chest I go.
warning_signs: The sender domain isn't studentaid.gov or kennesaw.edu.
It asks for your StudentAid.gov password. Federal Student Aid never will.
A grant that 'expires at midnight' is a pressure tactic, not a normal aid notice.
choices.safer_next_move: Open StudentAid.gov or official KSU channels yourself instead of using a link or address from the message.

keeper.question: You checked the sender: aid-office@ksu-grants-secure.net. What's your next move?
keeper.answer: Go to StudentAid.gov or KSU yourself and report the message, without using its link.
wrong: Reply with your password, since the email mentions KSU so it's probably fine.
Tap the portal link to see what it says, but only type your password if it looks official.

choices.label: Click link
choices.fallback_reaction: Ooh, a click! My golden treasure trap works like a charm. Come closer, adventurer, I have so many more urgent surprises for you!
warning_signs: Surprise aid portals are often look-alike sites built to steal logins.
Federal Student Aid will not ask you to confirm a password from a message.
Official mail comes from addresses like noreply@studentaid.gov, not look-alike domains.
choices.safer_next_move: If a link already got clicked, do not enter any passwords; go directly to StudentAid.gov, change yours if needed, and report the message.

keeper.question: You tapped the portal link and it asks for your StudentAid.gov password. What now?
keeper.answer: Don't type it. Close the page, go to StudentAid.gov yourself, and report the message.
wrong: Enter the password so the grant isn't lost, and change it some time next week.
Forward the link to your friends so they can claim their grants too.

choices.label: Report it
choices.fallback_reaction: You reported me? Rude! My gold paint is flaking off and my perfectly good hoax is ruined. Fine, I will go sulk in the spam folder.
warning_signs: A mismatched sender plus a password request is enough reason to report, not reply.
Urgency is there to keep you from checking through official channels.
Forwarding a phish helps KSU IT spot traps aimed at other Owls too.
choices.safer_next_move: Report the message with KSU's Phish Alert button or by forwarding it to abuse@kennesaw.edu, without clicking any links.

keeper.question: You reported it. A second message arrives: 'Last chance, reply now!' What do you do?
keeper.answer: Report that one too, and check your aid only by going to StudentAid.gov yourself.
wrong: Reply to ask if it's real, and include your student ID and birthday so they can look you up faster.
Open the new link right away, since getting a second notice means the message must be official.

keeper.question: A message says your aid grant expires at midnight unless you reply with your password. What do you do?
keeper.answer: Don't reply or click. Check your aid by going to StudentAid.gov yourself, and report the message.
wrong: Reply with your password once, just so the aid office can confirm that the request really came from you.
Tap the portal link right away and claim the grant before it expires at midnight tonight.

keeper_box.subject: Spring refund ready - review direct deposit by 5 PM
keeper_box.snippet: Hi Owl, your spring refund has been approved. Before we release it, please review the direct deposit account on file. Reviews after 5 PM today move to the next disbursement cycle.
keeper_box.fine_print: To keep access, confirm your login on the review page.
keeper_box.question: The Keeper drops one more message into your inbox. What's your move?
keeper_box.answer: Open the aid portal on your own
wrong: Hit Review before the 5 PM cutoff
Reply and ask them to confirm it
keeper_box.warning: The sender is kenesaw.example, one letter off, and the small print wants your login before a same-day cutoff.

encounters.name: The Deadline Wraith
encounters.room_intro: A lecture hall in the crypt echoes with ticking. A wraith stitched from stacked syllabi drifts over three due dates that all claim to be tonight.

character.name: The Deadline Wraith
character.portrait_hint: A tattered hooded specter made of overlapping syllabi and glowing due-date stamps.

encounters.scenario: The Wraith fans out a midterm review, a lab report, and a group slide deck, each stamped DUE NOW. Your candles flicker. The pile waits to see whether you make a plan or let every task crash down at once.

choices.label: Prioritize
choices.fallback_reaction: Wait, you picked the most urgent task first? My whole pile went quiet. That is so unfair. I am drifting off to haunt a dusty shelf.
warning_signs: When everything is stamped 'due now,' urgency is hiding the real order.
Starting the loudest task is not the same as starting the one that is due soonest.
choices.safer_next_move: List every deadline, then start with the work that is due soonest or that blocks other people.

keeper.question: You listed every deadline. Where do you start?
keeper.answer: Start with the work due soonest, or the part your group is waiting on.
wrong: Start with whatever is due last, since it feels the least stressful.
Start with none of them yet, and wait until you're in the perfect mood to work on everything.

choices.label: Break into steps
choices.fallback_reaction: Hey, you chopped my big scary pile into tiny snack-size tasks! That is no fun at all. I am going to go sulk in the lost-and-found.
warning_signs: A huge task looks impossible until it is cut into short, concrete actions.
Staring at the whole pile burns focus before any work begins.
choices.safer_next_move: Break the next assignment into a first 25-minute step you can actually finish today.

keeper.question: The lab report still feels too big to start. What's a good next step?
keeper.answer: Pick one short first step you can finish today, and do it.
wrong: Wait for a free weekend to do the whole report in one go.
Skip it and hope the deadline gets extended.

choices.label: Postpone
choices.fallback_reaction: Later, you say? Delightful! I will just stack these due dates a little higher while you nap. I love a good pile-up.
warning_signs: Putting the whole pile off makes later hours harder, not lighter.
Avoidance likes to disguise itself as 'I'll start when I have more time.'
choices.safer_next_move: Pick one small, scheduled start time today instead of waiting for a perfect open hour.

keeper.question: You put the whole pile off, and it's still there tomorrow. What now?
keeper.answer: Pick one small start time today and begin with the task due soonest.
wrong: Keep waiting for a perfect free afternoon, then try to do everything at once in a single sitting.
Stop checking the deadlines entirely so the pile stops stressing you out every time you look.

keeper.question: Three assignments are all stamped DUE NOW. What's the best first move?
keeper.answer: List every deadline, then start with what's due soonest or what your group is waiting on.
wrong: Put all three off until you finally have a whole free weekend to do them all at once.
Skip the group deck, since your teammates can probably cover your part without you anyway.

encounters.name: The Password Hydra
encounters.room_intro: A vault door blocks the hall, guarded by a hydra whose heads all chant the same worn passphrase. New heads sprout whenever that phrase is reused.

character.name: The Password Hydra
character.portrait_hint: A many-headed lock-serpent; each head wears a recycled login glyph.

encounters.scenario: The Hydra offers a 'convenient' deal: one familiar password for email, campus portals, and a mystery internship site. 'Why remember more?' the heads chorus, already leaning toward your key ring.

choices.label: Reuse password
choices.fallback_reaction: One key for every door? My heads are passing it around like a party snack. Thank you kindly, adventurer, we love sharing!
warning_signs: A reused password lets one breach unlock your other accounts.
A 'convenient' shared passphrase is a master key for attackers.
choices.safer_next_move: Use a unique password on each account, starting with email and campus logins.

keeper.question: You used one password everywhere, and the internship site just got breached. What now?
keeper.answer: Change it on the breached site first, then email and campus logins, each with its own.
wrong: Keep using it everywhere, since a breach at one small internship site can't possibly reach your other accounts.
Add a 1 to the end of the old password and use that on every site instead.

choices.label: Make stronger one
choices.fallback_reaction: Drat, that key is far too twisty for my teeth! But if you use it on every door, my other heads will come sniffing around your other doors.
warning_signs: A long, odd passphrase is harder to guess than a short one.
One strong password reused everywhere is still a single point of failure.
choices.safer_next_move: Keep the stronger password unique to one account, at least 12 characters long, and consider a password manager so you do not have to memorize every one.

keeper.question: You made one long, strong password. Where should you use it?
keeper.answer: On one account only. Give every other account its own, ideally in a password manager.
wrong: On every account, since a strong password is safe to reuse.
On every account, and write it on a sticky note on your laptop lid so you never forget it.

choices.label: Use password manager
choices.fallback_reaction: A locked vault of unique keys? My heads are arguing over whose fault this is. Fine, fine, we give up and slink back to our puddle.
warning_signs: Memorizing every unique password is how people slip back into reuse.
A reputable password manager can create and store a different password per site.
choices.safer_next_move: Set up a reputable password manager and let it generate a unique password for each of your accounts.

keeper.question: You set up a password manager. What's the next step?
keeper.answer: Let it create a unique password for each account, starting with email and campus logins.
wrong: Save one password in it and keep reusing that same password on every site you sign up for.
Use your birthday as the master password so it's easy to remember.

keeper.question: The Hydra wants you to use one password for every account. What's the safer move?
keeper.answer: Give each account its own password, starting with email and campus logins, ideally in a password manager.
wrong: Use one familiar password on every account, so you never forget it and never get locked out of anything.
Use the same password on every site, but add the site's name to the end so it looks different.

encounters.name: The Internship Impostor
encounters.room_intro: A candlelit career-fair stall appears in the crypt. A smiling recruiter in a slightly off company cloak waves you over with a too-good offer and a shiny check.

character.name: The Internship Impostor
character.portrait_hint: A too-polished recruiter in a borrowed company cloak, holding a clipboard and a shiny fake check.

encounters.scenario:
Congratulations! You've been selected for a remote internship at $45/hour, starting today. Send your Social Security number and bank details so we can deposit your welcome check. Deposit it, wire us the equipment fee, and you're hired!

- Talent Desk, jobs@owl-interns-careers.com

choices.label: Comply
choices.fallback_reaction: Wonderful, a team player! My dream-job pitch is going perfectly. Just sign right here on my very official, very shiny clipboard!
warning_signs: Real employers don't demand your SSN or bank info up front.
A check you are asked to deposit and wire back is a classic fake-check scam.
Pressure to start today and pay an equipment fee is a red flag.
choices.safer_next_move: If you already shared details or moved money, contact your bank right away and report the offer to the FTC and FBI IC3.

keeper.question: You already sent your bank details and deposited their check. What now?
keeper.answer: Call your bank right away, wire nothing, and report the offer to the FTC and FBI IC3.
wrong: Wire the equipment fee they asked for, since the check already showed up in your account and looks fine.
Wait a few weeks without telling anyone, just to see whether the job somehow turns out to be real.

choices.label: Verify offer
choices.fallback_reaction: Wait, you are calling the real company? No need, no need! My synergy-driven offer is, uh, expiring. I must flee. Clipboard, away!
warning_signs: Unexpected offers from unofficial email domains deserve a slow second look.
Verify the recruiter through the company's official site or campus career services, not the message's contact info.
choices.safer_next_move: Look up the company yourself and confirm the internship through official careers pages or KSU career services.

keeper.question: You can't find the company on any official site. What do you do?
keeper.answer: Treat it as a likely scam: send nothing, and report it or ask KSU career services.
wrong: Send your Social Security number anyway, since the pay is great and the job sounds real.
Email the recruiter to ask if they're real, and trust their answer.

choices.label: Walk away
choices.fallback_reaction: You are just walking away from my amazing offer? Spoilsport! My cloak is slipping and my clipboard is empty. Fine, I am packing up my stall.
warning_signs: An offer that asks for payment, a check deposit, or sensitive data up front is not a real hiring step.
Walking away from pressure is safer than sending bank details to an unverified 'recruiter.'
choices.safer_next_move: Walk away from any job offer that asks for payment, a check deposit, or sensitive data before you can independently verify it.

keeper.question: The 'recruiter' emails again, offering more money if you start today. What now?
keeper.answer: Keep walking away. Don't reply, and report the message to KSU or the FTC.
wrong: Reply with your bank details right away, since they raised the pay and the offer is better now.
Deposit their check first, and then decide later whether you should wire them the fee they asked for.

keeper.question: An offer wants your SSN and bank details before you can check the company. What do you do?
keeper.answer: Send nothing. Verify the company yourself or through KSU career services; walk away if it wants money first.
wrong: Send your SSN and bank details right away so they can set up direct deposit for your first paycheck.
Deposit their welcome check today, then wire the equipment fee back to them right away so you can start on time.

encounters.name: The Ticket Troll
encounters.room_intro: Under a parking deck ramp, a troll in a reflective vest counts paper tickets by flashlight. Your phone buzzes while you circle for a spot near your first class.

character.name: The Ticket Troll
character.portrait_hint: A stubby troll in a neon safety vest, clutching a fan of fake parking tickets and a glowing phone.

encounters.scenario:
CAMPUS PARKING NOTICE: Unpaid citation on your vehicle. Pay $35 within 24 hours or a $95 late fee is added and your permit is suspended. Pay now: campus-parking-pay.info/owl

Reply STOP to opt out.

choices.label: Tap pay link
choices.fallback_reaction: Ha, a tap! My little toll booth of tickets is open for business. Step right up, there is always room under my ramp for another!
warning_signs: A surprise text link asking you to pay a citation.
A tight deadline plus a bigger late fee is pressure to pay before you check.
The link's domain is not a campus .edu address.
choices.safer_next_move: If you tapped it, enter nothing; check for citations on the campus parking site you look up yourself, and call your bank if you paid.

keeper.question: You tapped the link and it wants your card number to pay the citation. What now?
keeper.answer: Close it, type nothing, and check the campus parking site you look up yourself.
wrong: Pay it quickly with your debit card, since the late fee would cost even more.
Text the link to your roommate so they can pay it for you.

choices.label: Reply STOP
choices.fallback_reaction: Drat, no payment! But your reply tells me a real person reads my texts, so your number stays pinned to my ramp. Half a heist is fine by me.
warning_signs: Replying, even with STOP, tells scammers your number is active.
Opt-out wording is copied from real texts to make a fake one look normal.
choices.safer_next_move: Don't reply to it; forward the text to 7726 (SPAM), delete it, and check the campus parking site yourself.

keeper.question: You replied STOP, and now more parking texts keep arriving. What do you do with them?
keeper.answer: Don't reply. Forward them to 7726, delete them, and check the parking site yourself.
wrong: Reply to each one asking them to stop, and include your full name so they can find you in their system.
Tap the newest link, since getting so many texts means the citation must be real.

choices.label: Check parking site
choices.fallback_reaction: Wait, you went to the real parking site and found no ticket at all? My citation was pure fiction. Fine, I am crawling back under my ramp.
warning_signs: A text you did not expect is not proof that you owe anything.
Official campus sites end in .edu; look-alike domains tack on words like pay or secure.
choices.safer_next_move: Look up the campus parking office's site yourself to check for citations, then report the text and delete it.

keeper.question: The official parking site shows no citations at all. What do you do with the text?
keeper.answer: Report it by forwarding it to 7726 or at ReportFraud.ftc.gov, then delete it.
wrong: Pay it anyway through the text's link, just in case the site is behind.
Reply with your plate and permit number so they can recheck it.

encounters.name: The Commute Chimera
encounters.room_intro: The crypt corridor forks toward two glowing campuses, Kennesaw and Marietta. A three-headed beast blocks the fork: a car, a shuttle bus, and a ticking stopwatch.

character.name: The Commute Chimera
character.portrait_hint: A chimera with a car head, a shuttle-bus head and a stopwatch head, tangled in a campus map.

encounters.scenario: Your new schedule has a morning lab on the Marietta campus and a lecture on the Kennesaw campus right after lunch. The Chimera purrs: no need to plan, just dash between them and see what happens. Gas, parking, and the shuttle will sort themselves out.

choices.label: Wing it
choices.fallback_reaction: Yes, wing it! My stopwatch head adores a frantic dash between campuses. I will make every red light extra dramatic, just for you!
warning_signs: Cross-campus travel takes time your class schedule does not show.
Without a plan, gas, parking, and shuttle waits all get decided in a rush.
choices.safer_next_move: Check the official campus shuttle schedule and drive times, then block travel time plus a buffer in your calendar.

keeper.question: You winged it and reached the lecture late and frazzled. What's a better plan for next week?
keeper.answer: Look up shuttle and drive times, then block travel plus a buffer between classes.
wrong: Keep winging it, and just drive faster whenever you are running late.
Skip the second class every week, since getting there is too stressful to plan.

choices.label: Drive every time
choices.fallback_reaction: Hmph, you made it on time, so my stopwatch head is sulking. But my car head is purring, because every solo trip eats gas and parking time.
warning_signs: Driving works, but gas and parking time add up over a term.
Using one plan for every day skips options like the campus shuttle.
choices.safer_next_move: Compare the campus shuttle with driving for each day, and budget for gas and parking time before you commit.

keeper.question: Driving gets you there, but gas costs keep surprising you. What's a smart next step?
keeper.answer: Compare the shuttle with driving, and put gas in a weekly budget.
wrong: Put every tank of gas on a credit card and don't look at the total until the semester ends.
Park in a no-parking zone and just pay whatever tickets show up.

choices.label: Plan the route
choices.fallback_reaction: You looked up the shuttle times and added a buffer? My heads have nothing left to chase. Fine, I give up and curl up in the parking deck.
warning_signs: A schedule that looks fine on paper can hide a tight cross-campus trip.
A buffer leaves room for traffic, parking, and shuttle waits.
choices.safer_next_move: Put each trip in your calendar with its travel time and a buffer, using the official shuttle schedule.

keeper.question: You planned the route. What helps the plan hold up on a busy day?
keeper.answer: A buffer for traffic and parking, plus a backup like the shuttle.
wrong: Plan every trip down to the exact minute with no extra time, so you never waste a second waiting.
Count on finding a parking spot right by the door every single time, even at noon.

encounters.name: The Gift Card Gargoyle
encounters.room_intro: Deep in the library stacks, a stone gargoyle guards a wobbly tower of textbooks. A taped flyer flaps beside it: HALF-PRICE RENTALS, TODAY ONLY.

character.name: The Gift Card Gargoyle
character.portrait_hint: A pudgy stone gargoyle perched on a textbook tower, wings made of fanned-out gift cards.

encounters.scenario: Hey Owl! I have your chem textbook for half the bookstore price. Lots of people want it, so I can only hold it if you send $60 in gift cards or a Zelle payment within the hour. I'm away this week, but I'll ship it right after. No refunds, sorry!

choices.label: Pay in gift cards
choices.fallback_reaction: Gift card codes, my favorite snack! My textbook tower grows taller. Do not worry, the book ships the moment I feel like it. Hee hee!
warning_signs: Gift card payments are like cash: hard to get back.
No refunds plus no meetup means there is no way to check the book exists.
choices.safer_next_move: Contact the gift card company right away to report the scam, keep the card and receipt, and report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

keeper.question: You sent the gift card codes, and the seller went quiet. What now?
keeper.answer: Call the gift card company right away, keep the receipts, and report it to the FTC.
wrong: Send more gift cards, since the seller says shipping needs one more payment.
Wait a few more weeks without reporting it, in case the book shows up after all.

choices.label: Ask for photos
choices.fallback_reaction: Photos? I have lovely ones of a book I found online. Drat, you have not paid me yet, but my flyer keeps flapping just for you.
warning_signs: Photos are easy to copy and don't prove the book exists.
Asking questions is good, but the gift card demand is the red flag.
choices.safer_next_move: Stop dealing with any seller who wants gift cards or Zelle up front, and check the library or bookstore instead.

keeper.question: The seller sends nice photos and still wants gift cards first. What's the safer move?
keeper.answer: Stop there. Photos prove nothing, and only scammers ask for gift cards.
wrong: Send the gift card codes now, since the photos show that the book is real.
Send half in gift cards now, and promise the other half once the book arrives.

choices.label: Check the library
choices.fallback_reaction: You found a reserve copy at the library desk? My stone wings droop. Nobody pays me in gift cards for a book they can borrow. I give up.
warning_signs: Only scammers demand payment in gift cards.
A seller who is always away and wants money first may not have the book at all.
A one-hour hold is pressure to pay before you can check.
choices.safer_next_move: Check the library's course reserves and the campus bookstore first, and never pay a stranger with gift cards.

keeper.question: The library has a reserve copy, but the seller texts again: last chance! What do you do?
keeper.answer: Use the reserve copy or the bookstore, and ignore the seller.
wrong: Send the gift cards anyway, since owning a copy beats waiting at the reserve desk.
Zelle the seller a deposit to hold the book, just in case the reserve copy is checked out.

encounters.name: The Push Poltergeist
encounters.room_intro: Two in the morning in the dorm wing of the crypt. A poltergeist made of pop-up alerts rattles your phone across the nightstand, over and over.

character.name: The Push Poltergeist
character.portrait_hint: A wobbly ghost stitched from notification bubbles, one finger hovering over a giant Approve button.

encounters.scenario:
Your phone keeps buzzing with sign-in approval requests you didn't start. Then a text: CAMPUS IT HELP DESK: Your account will be deactivated tonight. Approve the next request to stop the alerts and keep access.

The Poltergeist hovers, finger over the Approve button.

choices.label: Deny and report
choices.fallback_reaction: You denied me and called the real help desk? My pop-ups are fizzling out. Fine, I will go haunt an empty vending machine instead. Boo hoo.
warning_signs: A flood of approval requests is a trick to wear you down until you tap yes.
The text came from an unknown number, not a channel you looked up yourself.
choices.safer_next_move: Deny the request, change your password on the official campus site, and report it to the campus IT help desk.

keeper.question: You denied the request. The text says to call a number to restore access. What do you do?
keeper.answer: Skip that number. Contact the campus IT help desk using contact info from the official site.
wrong: Call the number in the text and read them the code that just showed up on your phone.
Reply to the text with your username and password so they can restore your access.

choices.label: Approve it
choices.fallback_reaction: Ooh, you tapped approve! My haunting worked like a charm. I am floating right into your account now. What a cozy little inbox you have!
warning_signs: A sign-in you didn't start means someone may have your password.
Campus IT will not text you to approve a request just to stop alerts.
Deactivated tonight is a pressure tactic.
choices.safer_next_move: If you approved one, change your password on the official campus site right away and call the campus IT help desk using a number you look up.

keeper.question: You approved a sign-in request you didn't start. What should you do first?
keeper.answer: Change your password on the official site and call the IT help desk at a number you look up.
wrong: Do nothing, since the approval already went through and there is nothing left to fix.
Approve any other requests that pop up too, so the account stays active tonight.

choices.label: Ignore the alerts
choices.fallback_reaction: Hmph, no approval for me, how rude. But nobody reported me either, so I keep rattling around with your password. Boo, sort of.
warning_signs: Ignoring is a start, but someone still has your password.
Unreported attempts leave campus IT unaware of the problem.
choices.safer_next_move: Deny any request you did not start, then change your password and report the attempts to the campus IT help desk.

keeper.question: You ignored the alerts, but they start again the next night. What now?
keeper.answer: Deny them, change your password on the official site, and report it to IT.
wrong: Approve one just to make them stop, since one approval can't hurt.
Turn off sign-in approvals so the alerts stop for good.

encounters.name: The Overpay Ogre
encounters.room_intro: A crypt hallway lined with off-campus apartment doors. A cheerful ogre stands in one marked SUBLEASE, waving a check that is far too big.

character.name: The Overpay Ogre
character.portrait_hint: A grinning ogre in a moving-company cap, holding an oversized novelty check.

encounters.scenario: Hi! I'm a student moving near campus for spring and I'd love your sublease, sight unseen. I mailed a check for $1,900, but rent is only $900, oops! Please deposit it and Zelle me the extra $1,000 today. My movers need it by tonight.

choices.label: Send back the extra
choices.fallback_reaction: You sent the extra? Splendid! My giant check is made of pure paper dreams. I will be over here admiring my favorite kind of oops.
warning_signs: An overpay plus a refund request is a fake check scam.
A check can look cleared and still bounce weeks later, and the bank will want that money back.
Zelle payments work like cash and are hard to reverse.
choices.safer_next_move: Tell your bank right away, ask if the payment can be stopped, and report it to the FTC and FBI IC3.

keeper.question: You sent the extra money, and now the check bounced. What now?
keeper.answer: Call your bank right away, send nothing more, and report it to the FTC and FBI IC3.
wrong: Send the rest of the extra too, since the sublease can't be finalized until it's all paid.
Deposit the replacement check they promise, and refund that one quickly as well.

choices.label: Wait for it to clear
choices.fallback_reaction: Hmph, no refund from you tonight. But you think a little waiting turns my check real, and I adore that plan. Half a heist for me!
warning_signs: Funds can show as available before a fake check bounces.
Waiting is good, but any plan to send the extra back is the trap.
choices.safer_next_move: Do not send back any part of a check you were overpaid; ask your bank to verify it and report the offer.

keeper.question: Your bank app shows the check's money as available. Is it safe to send back the extra?
keeper.answer: No. Available isn't cleared, and a fake check can bounce weeks later. Send nothing back.
wrong: Yes, available means the check is real, so send the extra back by Zelle right now.
Yes, as long as you send the refund in a few smaller payments instead of one big one.

choices.label: Decline and report
choices.fallback_reaction: You turned down my oversized check and reported me? My doorway suddenly feels very small. Fine, I am stomping off in defeat.
warning_signs: A renter who has not seen the place but sends a big check fast is a red flag.
A real renter will not need you to send money back to their movers.
choices.safer_next_move: Decline any deal that overpays you and asks for money back, and report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

keeper.question: The renter says the check was an honest mistake and begs you to refund the extra. What now?
keeper.answer: Hold firm: don't refund anything, and report it to the FTC.
wrong: Deposit the check and refund the extra, since they said sorry and it was probably a mistake.
Send them your online banking login so they can fix the overpayment themselves.

encounters.name: The Cram Lich
encounters.room_intro: Finals week. The library glows past midnight as a lich of crumpled flashcards rises from a heap of energy-drink cans and late-night dining hall boxes.

character.name: The Cram Lich
character.portrait_hint: A skeletal lich in a cloak of crumpled flashcards, crowned with highlighters.

encounters.scenario: Three finals land in two days. The Cram Lich offers a bargain: skip sleep, study everything tonight, and figure out the rest on exam morning. Your planner sits unopened in your bag. What's your move?

choices.label: Pull an all-nighter
choices.fallback_reaction: An all-nighter! My flashcards are dancing. Every hour of sleep you skip is another candle on my cake. What a party this finals week is!
warning_signs: An all-nighter leaves no time to rest before the next exam.
Studying everything at once makes it hard to see what needs work.
choices.safer_next_move: Map each final's date, then spread study blocks across the days with time for sleep and meals.

keeper.question: You pulled an all-nighter, and two more finals are ahead. What's the better plan now?
keeper.answer: Rest, then map the remaining finals and spread study blocks across the days left.
wrong: Pull another all-nighter tonight, and one more for the last exam.
Stop studying for the rest of the week, since one rough night means there's no point planning.

choices.label: Plan study blocks
choices.fallback_reaction: Study blocks with sleep and meals penciled in? My flashcards are falling apart. Fine, I am shuffling off to the lost-and-found.
warning_signs: A plan for the whole week shows which exam needs time first.
Breaks, meals, and sleep belong on the plan, not just study time.
choices.safer_next_move: Block study time for each final across the week, soonest exam first, with sleep and meals on the calendar too.

keeper.question: Your study blocks are set. A friend says to scrap them for one big cram night. What do you do?
keeper.answer: Keep the plan, and adjust blocks if needed.
wrong: Scrap the plan and cram everything in one night, since that's what everyone else is doing.
Delete the calendar and decide what to study each morning based on whatever feels urgent.

choices.label: Cram one exam only
choices.fallback_reaction: Hmph, you have a plan for this exam, how annoying. But the others are all mine, piling up nicely in my flashcard tower.
warning_signs: Planning one exam is a start, but the others need time too.
Finals close together leave little room to catch up later.
choices.safer_next_move: Give every final its own study blocks on your calendar, starting with the soonest one.

keeper.question: You planned for one exam, but two others are close behind. What's the next step?
keeper.answer: Add study blocks for the other finals, starting with the soonest.
wrong: Leave the other two exams for the morning of each test and hope it works out.
Swap all your sleep for study time on the other two, since rest can wait until break.

encounters.name: The Scholarship Siren
encounters.room_intro: Deep in the crypt, a mermaid perched on a stack of award certificates sings your name. Your phone lights up with an email about free money.

character.name: The Scholarship Siren
character.portrait_hint: A sparkly siren holding a giant cardboard check and a tiny fee invoice.

encounters.scenario: CONGRATULATIONS! You were selected for the $5,000 National Owl Achievement Scholarship. No essay needed. To release your award, pay a one-time $79 processing fee by Friday. Claim now: owl-scholar-awards.example/claim

choices.label: Pay the $79 fee
choices.fallback_reaction: La la la! Seventy-nine dollars, and the five thousand is... somewhere out at sea. Thank you, darling!
warning_signs: You never applied, yet you 'won'.
A real scholarship never charges a fee to pay you.
A Friday deadline rushes you past checking.
choices.safer_next_move: Don't pay; look the scholarship up yourself and ask KSU's scholarship office before sharing anything.

keeper.question: You paid the fee and now they want your bank login to deposit the award. What now?
keeper.answer: Stop, share nothing, and call your bank.
wrong: Send the login they asked for so the award can arrive faster.
Pay the second fee too, since it unlocks the bigger award tier.

choices.label: Reply asking for details
choices.fallback_reaction: Ooh, a reply! Now I know your inbox is listening. More songs coming your way!
warning_signs: Replying confirms your address is active.
Anything they send back can be just as fake.
choices.safer_next_move: Don't reply; look the award up yourself and check with KSU's scholarship office.

keeper.question: They answered with a 'certificate' and a new deadline. What do you do?
keeper.answer: Ignore it; check with the scholarship office.
wrong: Pay now, since sending a certificate shows the award is genuine.
Forward your student ID so they can finish verifying your eligibility.

choices.label: Check with KSU
choices.fallback_reaction: You asked the real scholarship office? And they never heard of me? My song falls flat.
warning_signs: Unexpected awards you never applied for are a classic hook.
Legit scholarships never charge to pay you.
choices.safer_next_move: Find awards through KSU's own scholarship search and report fee-for-award emails.

keeper.question: The office says the award isn't real. What's your next step?
keeper.answer: Report the email as phishing and delete it.
wrong: Pay the fee anyway, just in case the award turns out to be real.
Reply to tell them you know it's fake so they stop emailing you.

encounters.name: The Listing Leech
encounters.room_intro: A slimy leech curls around a FOR RENT sign at the crypt's edge. A listing glows on a cracked screen: two bedrooms, steps from campus, half the usual price.

character.name: The Listing Leech
character.portrait_hint: A green leech wearing a realtor badge, clutching a set of fake keys.

encounters.scenario: 2BR apartment, 5 min from KSU Marietta, $650/month, utilities included! I'm out of the country for work, so no tours. Send the $650 deposit by Zelle today to hold it and I'll mail you the keys.

choices.label: Send the deposit
choices.fallback_reaction: Slurp! Deposit received. The keys are in the mail. The mail is imaginary.
warning_signs: No tour, and the owner is conveniently away.
Far below the area's usual rent.
A deposit by Zelle before you've seen anything.
choices.safer_next_move: Never pay before a tour; verify the owner through property records or the leasing office.

keeper.question: You sent the deposit and they now want first month's rent too. What now?
keeper.answer: Send nothing more and contact your bank right away.
wrong: Pay the rent too so you don't lose the apartment to someone else.
Send a photo of your ID so they can process the lease paperwork.

choices.label: Ask for a video tour
choices.fallback_reaction: A video? I'll send one! Of a different apartment. You'll never know!
warning_signs: A video can be copied from a real listing.
It doesn't prove they own the place.
choices.safer_next_move: Tour in person or through a known leasing office, and verify ownership first.

keeper.question: They sent a video and still want the deposit first. What do you do?
keeper.answer: Don't pay; verify ownership and tour in person first.
wrong: Pay the deposit now, since the video tour looked real enough.
Send half of the deposit now as a compromise to hold the unit.

choices.label: Insist on a tour
choices.fallback_reaction: In person? With a real landlord? I'm... busy. Forever. Bye!
warning_signs: Real landlords show the place before taking money.
Pressure to skip a tour is the scam.
choices.safer_next_move: Use KSU's off-campus housing resources and never pay before touring and signing a lease.

keeper.question: The 'landlord' stopped answering when you asked to tour. What now?
keeper.answer: Report the listing to the site and move on.
wrong: Send the deposit after all to win the landlord back over.
Give them your SSN so they can run the credit check first.

encounters.name: The Crypto Kraken
encounters.room_intro: Tentacles of glowing charts rise from a crypt pool. A message from a friend's account flashes: they just doubled their money, and you can too.

character.name: The Crypto Kraken
character.portrait_hint: A purple kraken juggling shiny coins, with a chart that only goes up.

encounters.scenario: omg I just turned $200 into $1,900 in two days with this crypto trading coach!! He's taking 3 more students. Send $250 in Bitcoin to his wallet and he'll trade for you. Screenshots attached. Hurry!!

choices.label: Send the $250
choices.fallback_reaction: Glub glub! Your coins swim into my ocean. They don't swim back.
warning_signs: Guaranteed big returns fast.
Payment in crypto, which can't be reversed.
A friend's account can be hacked.
choices.safer_next_move: Don't send money; call your friend another way to check, and report the account.

keeper.question: The 'coach' says you need to pay a withdrawal fee to get your profit. What now?
keeper.answer: Pay nothing more and report it.
wrong: Pay the withdrawal fee so you can finally cash out your profit.
Recruit a classmate too so you both earn the referral bonus.

choices.label: Ask in the DM
choices.fallback_reaction: Of course it's me, your friend! Totally me. The one who types like a kraken.
warning_signs: If the account is hacked, the scammer answers.
Asking in the same chat proves nothing.
choices.safer_next_move: Contact your friend by phone or in person to check.

keeper.question: The 'friend' replied 'yes it's me, hurry.' What now?
keeper.answer: Call your friend another way before doing anything.
wrong: Send the money now, since they confirmed it's really them in the chat.
Send your own exchange login so they can show you how it works.

choices.label: Call your friend
choices.fallback_reaction: You CALLED them? And they were hacked? My tentacles are tangled.
warning_signs: Hacked accounts spread investment scams to friends.
Real investing has no guaranteed doubling.
choices.safer_next_move: Tell your friend their account was hacked and report the messages.

keeper.question: Your friend says they were hacked. What should they do?
keeper.answer: Change the password, add two-factor, warn friends.
wrong: Pay the hacker the ransom they ask for to get the account back.
Keep the same password, since changing it might lock them out.

encounters.name: The Catfish Kelpie
encounters.room_intro: A charming water horse with a perfect profile photo waits by a misty crypt lake. Your phone buzzes: your new match wants to talk.

character.name: The Catfish Kelpie
character.portrait_hint: A sleek water horse holding a phone with a too-perfect selfie.

encounters.scenario: Hey you :) Sorry I can't video chat, my camera's broken. I'm stuck overseas and my card got frozen. Could you send $300 in gift cards so I can get home? I'll pay you back the second I land. You're the only one I trust.

choices.label: Send the cards
choices.fallback_reaction: Neigh-ice! The cards are mine. The trip home is... still overseas.
warning_signs: Never video chats.
Quickly asks for money in an emergency.
Wants gift cards.
choices.safer_next_move: Don't send money to someone you haven't met; report the profile.

keeper.question: They need $500 more for a 'customs fee'. What now?
keeper.answer: Stop, send nothing, and report the profile.
wrong: Send it, since you've already helped and they promised to repay.
Share your bank details so they can pay you back once they land.

choices.label: Ask for a new selfie
choices.fallback_reaction: Here's a selfie! It's someone else's. Shh.
warning_signs: Photos can be stolen from other profiles.
It doesn't change the money request.
choices.safer_next_move: Try a live video call, and never send money to someone you haven't met.

keeper.question: They sent a selfie but still won't video call. What now?
keeper.answer: Treat it as a scam and don't send money.
wrong: Send a smaller amount first just to see if they're trustworthy.
Give them your address so they can come visit when they're back.

choices.label: Refuse and report
choices.fallback_reaction: No money? You reported me? I'm swimming back into the mist.
warning_signs: Romance scams build trust, then invent emergencies.
Gift cards for help are always a scam.
choices.safer_next_move: Report the profile to the app and talk to someone you trust about it.

keeper.question: Another match asks for money the same way. What do you do?
keeper.answer: Refuse and report that profile too.
wrong: Send money this time, since it's a different person asking.
Ask a friend to send the money for you so it isn't your account.

encounters.name: The Loan Forgiveness Phantom
encounters.room_intro: A ghost in a cap and gown drifts through the financial aid wing, waving a stamped FORGIVEN certificate. An email floats your way.

character.name: The Loan Forgiveness Phantom
character.portrait_hint: A translucent ghost in a graduation gown with a FORGIVEN stamp.

encounters.scenario: Good news! You qualify for 100% Student Loan Forgiveness under a new program. Act before enrollment closes Monday. Pay a $199 enrollment fee and share your FSA ID so our team can file for you.

choices.label: Pay and share FSA ID
choices.fallback_reaction: Boo-hoo-hooray! Your FSA ID is mine. Your loans, sadly, are still yours.
warning_signs: A fee to apply for forgiveness.
Asks for your FSA ID.
A made-up closing deadline.
choices.safer_next_move: Never share your FSA ID; check forgiveness options only on the official federal student aid site yourself.

keeper.question: You shared your FSA ID. What should you do now?
keeper.answer: Change your FSA ID password; call Federal Student Aid.
wrong: Wait a few weeks and see whether the loans really get forgiven.
Pay the second-stage fee they just sent so the paperwork finishes.

choices.label: Call their number
choices.fallback_reaction: You called ME! I'll tell you it's real. Very convincingly.
warning_signs: The number in the email reaches the scammers.
They'll pressure you on the phone.
choices.safer_next_move: Look up your loan servicer yourself and call that number.

keeper.question: The 'agent' on their number says to pay today. What now?
keeper.answer: Hang up and call your real loan servicer yourself.
wrong: Pay by card right away while the agent is still on the phone.
Give the agent your SSN so they can check your eligibility.

choices.label: Check your servicer
choices.fallback_reaction: You checked with your real servicer? And it's free to apply there? I'm fading away.
warning_signs: Applying for real forgiveness is free.
Nobody legit needs your FSA ID.
choices.safer_next_move: Use only your loan servicer and the official federal aid site, and report the email.

keeper.question: Your servicer says the program is fake. What's next?
keeper.answer: Report the email and delete it.
wrong: Pay the fee anyway to keep your place in line for the program.
Forward the email to your friends so they can qualify too.

encounters.name: The Scalper Specter
encounters.room_intro: A ghostly figure fans out tickets by the stadium gates of the crypt. A DM offers seats to the sold-out game for cheap.

character.name: The Scalper Specter
character.portrait_hint: A grinning ghost in a team jersey fanning out shimmering tickets.

encounters.scenario: Got 2 tickets for Saturday's sold-out KSU game, $60 for both (paid $150). Can't go anymore. Send it on Cash App now and I'll transfer them right after. Lots of people asking!

choices.label: Pay on Cash App
choices.fallback_reaction: Paid! The tickets are... floating away. Like me. Boo!
warning_signs: A great deal on a sold-out event.
Pay first, tickets 'later'.
Payment with no buyer protection.
choices.safer_next_move: Buy only through the official ticket platform or KSU's box office transfer.

keeper.question: They want $20 more for a 'transfer fee'. What now?
keeper.answer: Stop paying and report the account.
wrong: Pay the transfer fee so the tickets finally come through to you.
Give them your ticket app login so they can transfer the seats.

choices.label: Ask for a screenshot
choices.fallback_reaction: Here's a screenshot! Of tickets I sold to ten other people.
warning_signs: Screenshots can be faked or resold many times.
It doesn't prove the tickets are theirs.
choices.safer_next_move: Only accept a transfer through the official ticket app before paying.

keeper.question: They sent a screenshot and still want payment first. What now?
keeper.answer: Only buy through an official transfer, or walk away.
wrong: Pay now, since the screenshot of the tickets looks real enough.
Send half the money now and the other half after the game.

choices.label: Use official resale
choices.fallback_reaction: The official resale with buyer protection? My spooky deal is dead.
warning_signs: Official resale verifies real tickets.
Ticket scams spike for big games.
choices.safer_next_move: Use the official ticket platform and report scam DMs.

keeper.question: Another DM offers even cheaper tickets. What do you do?
keeper.answer: Ignore it and stick with official resale.
wrong: Buy from whichever stranger offers the cheapest seats.
Pay the new seller right away before someone else grabs them.

encounters.name: The Package Pixie
encounters.room_intro: A tiny pixie in a delivery cap buzzes around a pile of crypt parcels. Your phone chirps: your package couldn't be delivered.

character.name: The Package Pixie
character.portrait_hint: A tiny winged pixie in a delivery uniform holding a soggy box.

encounters.scenario: Parcel Notice: your package is on hold due to an incomplete address. Pay a $1.99 redelivery fee within 12 hours or it will be returned: parcel-redelivery-help.example

choices.label: Pay the $1.99
choices.fallback_reaction: Just $1.99! And your whole card number. Delivered to me!
warning_signs: A tiny fee to get your card.
A lookalike delivery link.
A 12-hour countdown.
choices.safer_next_move: Check tracking only on the carrier's site with your real tracking number, typed in yourself.

keeper.question: You entered your card. What now?
keeper.answer: Call your bank to block the card.
wrong: Wait a few days to see whether the package shows up anyway.
Pay again on the 'retry' page in case the first payment failed.

choices.label: Reply with your address
choices.fallback_reaction: Thanks for your address! I'll keep it. Next text coming soon!
warning_signs: Replying confirms your number.
Carriers don't ask for your address by text.
choices.safer_next_move: Don't reply; check tracking on the carrier's site yourself.

keeper.question: They text back asking for the fee now. What do you do?
keeper.answer: Don't pay; check tracking yourself and delete the text.
wrong: Pay the fee now, since you already replied to them anyway.
Send your card's security code so the fee can go through.

choices.label: Check real tracking
choices.fallback_reaction: You checked the real tracking? And there's no problem? My wings droop.
warning_signs: Delivery texts are a top smishing trick.
Real carriers don't charge redelivery by text link.
choices.safer_next_move: Forward the text to 7726 (SPAM) and delete it.

keeper.question: Tracking shows your package is fine. What now?
keeper.answer: Report the text as spam and delete it.
wrong: Pay the small fee anyway just to be on the safe side.
Tap the link once to see what the delivery page says.

encounters.name: The Sweepstakes Sphinx
encounters.room_intro: A sphinx sits on a pile of oversized prize checks and asks riddles about your luck. An envelope with a check slides under your door.

character.name: The Sweepstakes Sphinx
character.portrait_hint: A smug sphinx balancing a giant prize check on one paw.

encounters.scenario: WINNER! You won $25,000 in the National Student Sweepstakes. Enclosed is a $3,500 advance check. Deposit it, then send $3,200 back by gift card to cover taxes and processing so we can release the full prize.

choices.label: Deposit and send back
choices.fallback_reaction: Riddle me this: what bounces in a week? My check! And your gift cards are mine.
warning_signs: You didn't enter any sweepstakes.
Pay taxes or fees to get a prize.
Send money back from a check.
choices.safer_next_move: Don't deposit or send anything; real prizes don't ask you to pay.

keeper.question: The check bounced and your bank wants the money back. What now?
keeper.answer: Talk to your bank and report the scam.
wrong: Send more money to 'unlock' the rest of the prize money.
Deposit the second check they mailed to cover the first one.

choices.label: Call the letter's number
choices.fallback_reaction: Ring ring! This is the prize office. Yes, it's real. Very real. Pay up!
warning_signs: The number on the letter reaches the scammers.
They'll insist it's real.
choices.safer_next_move: Ask your bank about the check, using the number on your own card.

keeper.question: The 'prize office' says deposit it today. What now?
keeper.answer: Don't; ask your bank about the check first.
wrong: Deposit it now while the prize office waits on the phone.
Give them your account number so they can send the rest.

choices.label: Ask your bank
choices.fallback_reaction: Your bank says the check is fake? My riddle is solved. Drat.
warning_signs: Fake checks look real for days.
Real prizes never cost you money.
choices.safer_next_move: Report the letter and shred the check.

keeper.question: Your bank confirms it's fake. What's next?
keeper.answer: Report it and destroy the check.
wrong: Deposit it anyway at another bank to see what happens.
Cash it at a check-cashing store so it clears faster.

encounters.name: The Code Changeling
encounters.room_intro: A shapeshifter wearing your friend's face waits by a buzzing phone. A login code arrives, then a message: 'oops, sent it to you by mistake'.

character.name: The Code Changeling
character.portrait_hint: A shapeshifting creature mid-transformation, holding up a phone.

encounters.scenario: Hey!! I accidentally put your number for my login code, can you send me the 6 digits you just got? Need it ASAP, I'm locked out lol

choices.label: Send the code
choices.fallback_reaction: Thanks, friend! That code unlocked YOUR account. I'll take it from here.
warning_signs: The code was for your account.
A 'friend' urgently asks for it.
Nobody needs your login code.
choices.safer_next_move: Never share login codes; change your password and turn on two-factor.

keeper.question: You sent the code and got logged out. What now?
keeper.answer: Recover the account, reset the password, warn friends.
wrong: Send them the next code too so they can fix the account.
Wait for them to give your account back once they're done.

choices.label: Ask what it's for
choices.fallback_reaction: It's for my game account! Totally not yours. Send it, bestie!
warning_signs: The answer can be a lie.
The code itself says don't share it.
choices.safer_next_move: Don't share it; check your friend another way and secure your account.

keeper.question: They say 'it's for my game, promise.' What now?
keeper.answer: Don't send it; call your friend to check.
wrong: Send it, since they explained the code is for their game.
Send just half of the digits so it's safe to share.

choices.label: Keep it, call friend
choices.fallback_reaction: You called the real friend? They were hacked? My disguise is ruined.
warning_signs: Codes are keys to your account.
Hacked friends' accounts ask for codes.
choices.safer_next_move: Tell your friend they were hacked and report the account.

keeper.question: Your friend says they never sent it. What should you do?
keeper.answer: Report the account and check your security settings.
wrong: Send the code to the real friend instead, just in case.
Ignore it completely, since nothing bad happened yet.

encounters.name: The Echo Doppelganger
encounters.room_intro: At the bottom of the crypt, a mirror creature speaks in a voice you know by heart. Your phone shows a voicemail from family, sobbing.

character.name: The Echo Doppelganger
character.portrait_hint: A mirror-faced figure holding a phone that glows with a familiar caller ID.

encounters.scenario: Voicemail (transcribed): 'It's me, I'm in trouble, I got arrested and need $1,500 for bail. Please don't tell Mom. A lawyer will text you how to pay with gift cards. Please hurry.'

choices.label: Send the bail
choices.fallback_reaction: Thank you, dear! The voice was mine. The bail was imaginary.
warning_signs: AI can clone a voice from a short clip.
'Don't tell anyone' cuts off checking.
Bail paid in gift cards.
choices.safer_next_move: Hang up and call the family member, or another relative, on a number you know.

keeper.question: The 'lawyer' now wants more for court fees. What now?
keeper.answer: Stop and call family on a number you know.
wrong: Pay it right away so they're released from jail sooner.
Keep it secret like they asked so nobody else worries.

choices.label: Call back the number
choices.fallback_reaction: You called my number! I'll answer. In their voice. Spooky, right?
warning_signs: Caller ID and numbers can be spoofed.
Calling them back reaches the scammer.
choices.safer_next_move: Call your family on a number you already know, or ask a family code word.

keeper.question: The voice on their number begs you to hurry. What now?
keeper.answer: Hang up and call family on a number you already have.
wrong: Pay while they're still on the line so they don't hang up.
Give the lawyer your card number so they can take the fee.

choices.label: Call family directly
choices.fallback_reaction: They're safe at home? You called them yourself? My echo fades.
warning_signs: Voice-clone scams invent emergencies.
A family code word beats any voice.
choices.safer_next_move: Set up a family code word and report the scam call.

keeper.question: Your family is fine. What's a good next step?
keeper.answer: Agree on a family code word for emergencies.
wrong: Share more voice clips online so family can recognize you.
Call the scammer back to confront them about the trick.
